about: English meaning written for this library (en-scriptures): written from each mantra, its word meanings, Monier-Williams and Apte and Śaṅkara's reading, then reviewed, copy-audited and checked again against the mantra (docs/HOW-TO.md, Write our own meanings for a Sanskrit work); one piece per verse line, other readings in footnotes. [meaning, [footnotes]]

shanti.1: Om. May my speech be established in my mind.
May my mind be established in my speech.
O self-luminous Lord, be revealed to me.
Speech and mind, may you two bring the Veda to me.
May what I have heard (and learnt) never leave me.
With this study I join my days and nights together.
I shall speak ṛta, what is right; I shall speak the truth.
May that (Brahman) protect me; may it protect the speaker (the teacher).
May it protect me; may it protect the speaker.
1.1.1: Om. In the beginning this (world) was the Self (ātman) alone, one only;
there was nothing else at all that stirred.
He thought: Let me now create the worlds.
1.1.2: That Ambhas, the world of waters, lies beyond heaven, and heaven is its support;
the mid-air is Marīci, the world of rays; the earth is Mara, the world of death;
and the worlds below it are Āpaḥ, the waters.
1.1.3: He thought: Here now are the worlds;
let me now create the guardians of the worlds.
From the waters themselves he drew out a person (a body in human form) and gave him solid shape.
1.1.4: He brooded over him with tapas, his resolve.
As he was brooded over, a mouth broke open, like an egg; from the mouth came speech, and from speech fire (Agni).
The nostrils broke open; from the nostrils came breath (prāṇa), and from breath the wind (Vāyu).
The eyes broke open; from the eyes came sight, and from sight the sun (Āditya).
The ears broke open; from the ears came hearing, and from hearing the quarters of space.
The skin broke open; from the skin came the hairs, and from the hairs herbs and trees.
The heart broke open; from the heart came the mind, and from the mind the moon.
The navel broke open; from the navel came apāna, the downward breath, and from apāna death.
The organ of generation broke open; from it came seed, and from seed the waters.
1.2.1: He subjected him (the person) to hunger and thirst.
The deities said to him: Find us a dwelling
in which we may abide and eat food.
1.2.2: He brought them a cow. They said: This is surely not enough for us.
He brought them a horse. They said: This is surely not enough for us.
1.2.3: He brought them a person. They said: Oh, this is well made!
The person indeed is well made. He said to them: Enter, each into your own dwelling.
1.2.4: Fire, becoming speech, entered the mouth.
The wind, becoming breath, entered the nostrils.
The sun, becoming sight, entered the eyes.
The quarters of space, becoming hearing, entered the ears.
Herbs and trees, becoming the hairs, entered the skin.
The moon, becoming the mind, entered the heart.
Death, becoming apāna, entered the navel.
The waters, becoming seed, entered the organ of generation.
1.2.5: Hunger and thirst said to him: Find a place for the two of us as well.
He said to them: I give you two a share in these very deities; I make you sharers in them.
That is why, to whatever deity an oblation is taken up,
hunger and thirst are sharers in it.
1.3.1: He thought: Here now are the worlds and the guardians of the worlds; let me create food for them.
1.3.2: He brooded over the waters; from the waters so brooded over a form (a solid shape) was born.
The form that was born, that indeed is food.
1.3.3: This food, once created, turned away and sought to flee.
The person sought to seize it with speech, but he could not seize it with speech.
Had he seized it with speech, he would have been satisfied with food merely by speaking.
1.3.4: He sought to seize it with the breath, but he could not seize it with the breath.
Had he seized it with the breath, he would have been satisfied with food merely by smelling.
1.3.5: He sought to seize it with sight, but he could not seize it with sight.
Had he seized it with sight, he would have been satisfied with food merely by seeing.
1.3.6: He sought to seize it with hearing, but he could not seize it with hearing.
Had he seized it with hearing, he would have been satisfied with food merely by hearing.
1.3.7: He sought to seize it with the skin, but he could not seize it with the skin.
Had he seized it with the skin, he would have been satisfied with food merely by touching.
1.3.8: He sought to seize it with the mind, but he could not seize it with the mind.
Had he seized it with the mind, he would have been satisfied with food merely by thinking.
1.3.9: He sought to seize it with the organ of generation, but he could not seize it with the organ of generation.
Had he seized it with the organ of generation, he would have been satisfied with food merely by emitting.
1.3.10: He sought to seize it with apāna, and he seized it.
This air (vāyu) is the seizer of food; this air indeed lives by food (annāyu).
1.3.11: He thought: How could this (body) be without me?
He thought: By which of the two ways shall I enter it?
if apāna has drawn food in,
if the organ of generation has emitted,
1.3.12: He split open this very boundary, the suture of the skull,
and entered (the body) by that door.
This is the door called vidṛti, the cleft;
it is the nāndana, the place of joy.
1.3.13: Born (in the body), he looked around at the beings
and thought: What else here, other than me, is there to speak of?
He saw this very person as Brahman, the Absolute,
and said: I have seen this!
1.3.14: Therefore he is called Idandra, the one who sees this;
Him who is Idandra people call Indra,
For the gods are, as it were, fond of the veiled;
for the gods are, as it were, fond of the veiled.
2.1.1: Om. In a man this (self) first becomes a germ.
This, which is seed, is drawn from all the limbs:
it is their vigour, gathered together.
He bears his own self in himself.
When he pours it into a woman, he begets it;
2.1.2: It becomes one with the woman, just like a limb of her own.
Therefore it does not hurt her. She nourishes this self of her husband that has come here, into her.
2.1.3: She who nourishes is to be nourished. The woman bears that embryo.
He, the father, nurtures the child from the very first, from its birth onward.
In nurturing the child from its birth onward,
he nurtures his own self, for the continuance of these worlds.
For thus these worlds are kept unbroken. That is its second birth.
2.1.4: This self of his (the son) is put in his place for the doing of holy works.
Then this other self of his (the father), having done what was to be done and grown old, departs.
Departing from here, he is born again; that is his third birth.
2.1.5: This has been said by the seer:
While still in the womb I came to know all the births of these gods.
A hundred citadels of iron held me down; like a hawk I flew out of them with speed.
Lying in the womb itself, Vāmadeva spoke thus.
2.1.6: Knowing thus, he rose up and out when this body broke apart,
and in that heavenly world, having attained all desires,
3.1.1: Om. Who is this Self whom we worship?
Which of the two is that Self?
or that by which one hears,
or that by which one smells odours,
or that by which one utters speech,
or that by which one knows the sweet and the unsweet?
3.1.2: That which is the heart, and this mind —
awareness, the power to command, knowledge of the arts, consciousness, retentive power, perception, steadiness, thought, independence of thought,
distress of mind, memory, conception, determination, life, desire and longing —
all these are names of consciousness (prajñāna).
3.1.3: This (consciousness) is Brahmā, this is Indra, this is Prajāpati; it is all these gods,
and these five great elements: earth, air, space, water and light;
and these, mingled as it were with the small creatures; and seeds (sources of birth) of one kind and of another;
those born of eggs, born of wombs, born of moisture and born of sprouts;
whatever here has breath, that moves or flies,
all that has consciousness for its eye and is established in consciousness.
The world has consciousness for its eye; consciousness is its foundation.
3.1.4: By this conscious Self he rose up and out from this world,
and in that heavenly world, having attained all desires,

shanti.1: The śānti mantra of the Upaniṣads of the Ṛgveda. Peace is said three times: for the three kinds of affliction, from within oneself, from other beings and from the gods (fate).
1.2.1: In Śaṅkara's reading the great ocean is saṃsāra, the round of birth and death.
1.3.10: Here apāna is the breath that draws food in through the mouth (Śaṅkara), not the downward breath of the navel (1.1.4).
1.3.12: In Śaṅkara's reading the three dwellings are the right eye in waking, the mind in dream and the space of the heart in deep sleep; or the father's body, the mother's womb and one's own body. All three states are dreams, because in them the Self does not know its own nature.
1.3.14: The repeated words mark the end of the first chapter.
2.1.5: This is a mantra of the Ṛgveda (4.27.1). In Śaṅkara's reading the hundred citadels of iron are the many bodies.
2.1.6: The repeated words mark the end of the second chapter.
In Śaṅkara's reading the heavenly world here is not the heaven won by rites but Brahman, the Self's own nature.
3.1.4: The repeated words mark the end of the third chapter and of the Upaniṣad.
In Śaṅkara's reading the heavenly world here is not the heaven won by rites but Brahman, the Self's own nature.
